items.explain: They never get the chest X-ray because nobody could contact them, and they had missed an earlier follow-up.
They go back to sleeping under a bridge in winter because the shelter is full.
They are told to move along again and street crews take away their bedding.

items.plain: Can't get benefits or bank account
items.explain: They fail to restore income or open an account without an address, and their old job is gone to robots.
They end up in emergency care with a serious untreated lung illness after weight loss and night sweats.
They die from lung disease, made worse by cold and hunger.
They are expected to die at 49 from an untreated lung illness worsened by exposure and malnutrition.
They stay low on the housing list, keep slipping back, and are never offered a home.
Their main volunteer contact moves away for university, and their Sunday shelter visits stop.
The library where they spend their days becomes less welcoming, weakening their daily routine.
They have no prescription or address, so their high blood pressure stays untreated, with occasional clinic walk-ins.
They suffer a stroke while sleeping rough in the cold and are likely discharged back onto the street.
They die without a home, and a sibling is told through old library emails.
They are expected to die at 70 from a blood-pressure stroke worsened by cold while homeless.
They come under children's services assessment, citing mould, the child's wheeze and neighbour complaints.
Debt collectors add another deduction, leaving them too little to live on with their child.
Their benefits are cut a third time over a missed appointment or late form caused by childcare problems.
They occasionally join local tenants' meetings about repairs, limited by long work hours.
They are moved to temporary housing while mould is fixed, disrupting their child's schooling.
They stay on antidepressants long-term and stuck in care work with no guaranteed hours.
Their child moves out, they live alone, and child-related benefits stop.
They leave care work worn out in body and heart, and move onto sickness benefits.
They are expected to die at 66 from heart disease worsened by stress, poverty and likely smoking.
Their protest permit is likely approved with conditions, and a small tenants' gathering follows.
They refuse to pay a service charge in protest, and with other debts face formal arrears action.
Their tenants' group becomes a formal association, and they write more letters to the housing office.
They return to low-paid driving or agency work after a long gap, with wages docked for debts.
They drift away from activism as members leave and money worries continue.
They are guessed to have a heart problem in late middle age, though no medical records exist.
They are expected to die at 72 from heart disease diagnosed late, with no medical history recorded.
Their bank freezes the account over unexplained cash deposits, pushing them further into cash-only life.
They are arrested again for theft or drug-related crime through a shady local network.
They get a short prison sentence or a suspended one with an electronic tag and curfew.
They lose their rented room during the court case and depend on already-full shelters.
With local jobs automated and a criminal record, they look for agency warehouse work in another town.
They fall into cycles of cash-in-hand work and repeated run-ins with police.
They die in mid-life, most likely from drugs or violence.
They are expected to die at 44 from drug poisoning, or possibly injuries from an assault.
They keep lowering their methadone dose under supervision and stay clean through the year.
They meet their daughter and grandson again at Christmas and start seeing them a bit more.
They are turned down as a reading volunteer after a background check, with nothing else offered.
They are repeatedly stopped and searched by police without charge, causing ongoing strain.
Their cash-in-hand scrapyard job ends, leaving them on benefits only.
They start using illegal opioids again, now with lower tolerance and higher overdose risk.
They are arrested for theft or drug possession and get their thirteenth conviction.
They are expected to die at 64 from an opioid overdose after relapsing, worsened by years of drug use.
Their daughter leaves for university, and the household grows quieter and more distant.
Their supervisory job shrinks with automation, and they leave the company by resigning or being restructured.
Their marriage ends after the spouse grows close to a colleague and counselling fails.
They sell the family home and move out of town for a lower-level job.
They drink more, get diagnosed with high blood pressure, and have ongoing sleep problems.
Their career stalls in a shrinking, automated field and they settle on lower pay.
They have a major heart or blood-vessel event after years of high blood pressure and drinking.
They are expected to die at 67 from a stroke caused by high blood pressure and alcohol.
Their closest family member, their daughter, leaves for university, and they pay for the move.
Their messaging with a colleague turns into an emotional affair that becomes their main comfort.
They sell the family home in the divorce and rent nearby to stay close to work.

items.plain: Goes back to more teaching hours
items.explain: They increase their teaching hours to afford housing on one income.
They move in with a new partner, probably the colleague, and home life settles down.
They retire after a long teaching career and stay living in town.

items.plain: Dies of heart trouble, old age
items.explain: They are expected to die at 81 from a normal age-related heart problem, having stayed healthy.
They leave home to study social work, partly paid for by their father.
Their parents split up during their first year, and they drift further from their mother.
They finish their degree and become a registered social worker focused on housing and homelessness.
They come back to the area to work on local housing and child welfare cases.
They formally question how the housing list decides who gets homes and support tenant campaigns.
They burn out from heavy caseloads and cut their hours or leave the field.
They become the main unpaid carer for their elderly father.
They are expected to die at 77 from heart disease linked to high blood pressure.
They stop leaving home, stop visiting the memorial bench, and stop picking up antidepressants.
They change their will without a lawyer, apparently putting their affairs in order.
The neighbour's daughter who ran their errands moves away, and nobody else keeps watch.
Weight loss and depression lead to a fall, dehydration or malnutrition and an emergency hospital stay.
Their distant child is called and a care home is suggested, though they will likely refuse.
They die at home after neglecting themselves and stopping treatment, with heart problems in the background.
They are expected to die at 85 from self-neglect, grief-driven depression and weight loss, plus heart problems.
Their engagement ends because the partner's job secrecy stops them answering the person's questions.
They push further to uncover how computers decide housing, through appeals or outside contacts, keeping paper notes.

items.plain: Trouble at work, may be moved
items.explain: Their relationship with workplace IT sours over their questions, and they may be moved or lose access.
They leave town for somewhere unknown, with few ties left behind.
They stay informally in touch with a young social work student about housing and system fairness.
Their later life can't be predicted, with no settled job or home on record.
They are expected to die at 80 from ordinary age-related causes, likely heart-related.
They complete an automation project that eliminates 44 jobs, strengthening their standing with company bosses.
Their relationship ends because job secrecy prevents honest answers, and they move into a flat alone.
In an unlikely scenario, they reveal secret project details to their partner and face disciplinary action.
They sign a renewed data-sharing deal and become locked in as the link between company and council.
They are promoted to a regional role and partly relocate while still overseeing local operations.
They are found to have stress-related high blood pressure at a work check-up and take medication.
They retire on a good pension and live alone with few friends outside work.
They are expected to die at 78 from heart disease after years of high blood pressure.
